I’ve written the book as content/books/nutrition-science: 11 chapters, 34 sections, 264 quiz questions and about 13,000 words. Delivery is one tar.gz (attached above) to extract at the repo root.

I couldn’t run the .NET content processor here, so the book hasn’t gone through your real build. Instead I checked every file with a Python script that applies the same rules the compiler enforces: valid ids, at least two options, at least one correct answer, no single question with more than one correct answer, and valid YAML. All files pass. Run dotnet run --project tools/ObserverMagazine.ContentProcessor once to confirm.

Accuracy caveats

Sources: every section ends with a sources list, but I wrote the citations from memory. DOI links are included only where I was confident of them, but I didn’t open each one to confirm it resolves; the rest are plain author/journal/year references. Spot-check the DOI links before publishing.
Recent facts I looked up: the January 2026 US Dietary Guidelines, the April 2026 approval of the Foundayo weight-loss pill, and the 2024 bird flu findings in raw milk.
How the book handles certainty

Every major claim gets one of four grades: Established, Strong, Uncertain or Not supported. The grading scale is set out in chapter 1, and chapter 11 has a scorecard summarising all of them.
Raw milk, cow urine and dung remedies, detoxes, alkaline diets, seed-oil scares, the carnivore diet, homeopathy and similar claims are graded Not supported, with the evidence for each grade.
Where the science is open (eggs, sweeteners, the gut microbiome, fasting, full-fat dairy) the book says so plainly.
